claims.text: Introducing a controlled amount of Mn into a CrCoNi-based magnetic alloy will increase its coercive field.
The initial CrCoNi alloy is predominantly single-phase FCC.
The initial CrCoNi alloy has relatively low magnetic frustration.
A portion of a CrCoNi constituent can be replaced with Mn while retaining the alloy's high-entropy character.
The coercivity-enhancing effect should hold when the Mn-modified alloy remains single phase.
The effect should hold from ambient to cryogenic temperatures.
Mn incorporation causes local lattice distortions and variations in magnetic exchange interactions.
Mn incorporation enhances magnetic frustration and magnetic inhomogeneity.
Mn-induced magnetic inhomogeneity forms localized regions of increased magnetic anisotropy that act as pinning centers.
Mn disrupts otherwise uniform magnetic exchange interactions in the CrCoNi matrix.
Mn-induced frustration creates domain-wall pinning sites.
The pinning sites increase resistance to domain-wall motion.
Greater resistance to domain-wall motion produces a higher coercive field.
Under matched measurement conditions, the Mn-modified alloy will have a measurably higher coercive field than undoped CrCoNi.
A finite optimal Mn concentration range exists for improving coercivity.
Excessive Mn may cause phase segregation or structural transformations that counteract magnetic hardening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is expressly limited to Mn concentrations that preserve a single phase, yet phase segregation or transformation is itself listed as a falsifying result. Such a result instead places the tested sample outside the stated conditions and does not falsify the conditional coercivity claim.
